column2: I walk out among the herd to choose a warhorse. The grooms lead the best of the young stallions past me one by one, and I look them over with an eye trained since childhood: the depth of the chest, the set of the legs, the fire in the eye. One of them stands apart from the rest, strong and proud, and does not shy when I take its head.\n\nAs I swing up into the saddle I know I have chosen well. All that remains is to give it a name worthy of the steppe.

[Root.GetWarhorseName], my warhorse, has run its last gallop across the steppe and lain down for the long sleep. It carried me through raids and migrations, through snow and dust and the smoke of burning towns. It is time to say farewell to an old friend.

I have not been myself these last few weeks. Each morning I go out to the horse lines from habit, and each morning there is an empty place where [Root.GetWarhorseName] used to stand. It feels as if a piece of me is missing.
I must carry this burden alone.
I am lucky to have a [Root.Spouse.GetHusbandWife] to comfort me.
I am lucky to have a friend to comfort me.

My ward [ward_cant_ride.GetFirstName] is nearly eight summers old and still cannot sit a horse properly. Children of the camp half [ward_cant_ride.GetHerHis] age gallop circles around [ward_cant_ride.GetHerHim] and laugh. It is a disgrace to my yurt.
This will not do! I shall teach [ward_cant_ride.GetHerHim] myself.

Riding from one of my camps to the next, we come to a river swollen with the spring melt, its rapids white and violent. The way around would cost us days, so we must cross. I watch from the bank as the party picks its way down into the churning water. [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetFirstName], my [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetHusbandWife], rides [Root.GetWarhorseName], my own warhorse.\n\nThen it happens. [Root.GetWarhorseName] loses its footing in the rapids, [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetFirstName] is thrown from the saddle, and the current takes them both. I have a heartbeat to act before they are swept away, and I cannot save them both...

I dragged [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetFirstName] out of the river by the hair. [Root.GetWarhorseName] is gone, carried off downstream, but my [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetHusbandWife] is safe. [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetSheHeCap] is shaking with cold and fright, and cannot stop thanking me for the rescue.

I dragged [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetFirstName] out of the river by the hair. Once on the bank, [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetSheHe] gets to [spouse_danger_nomad_river_crossing.GetHerHis] feet, dripping and shivering, and rounds on me: 'You fool! I can swim! How could you let a horse like that drown?'
I, too, now question my choice.

One of the warriors of my retinue has come to my tent with a plea. Sickness has gone through the warrior's herd: most of the family's mares are dead, there is no milk for the children, and the winter grazing is still months away.
You shall have six mares from my own herd.
A pity, but I cannot help you.

I was about to leave [Root.GetWarhorseName] at the watering hole when [From.GetFirstName]'s horse stretched out its neck and bit it, hard, on the shoulder. [Root.GetWarhorseName] screamed and reared, and [From.GetFirstName] only laughed.
There is a better watering spot over here...

A painter from the settled lands rode into my camp today with a pack-mule of brushes and pigments. The painter has painted the lords of many great houses, or so the boast goes, and would be honoured to paint whatever the [Root.GetTitle] wishes.
